title: Overloading, overriding and dispatch
idea: Polymorphism lets one call behave differently per object: the compiler picks an overload from static types, then the JVM picks the override from the runtime class.

analogy.text: Overloading is a post room sorting parcels by the label on the box, not what is inside. Overriding is phoning a desk: whoever sits there now answers.
analogy.breaks: An object's class never changes after it is created.

points: Overloads share a name but differ in parameters; the compiler chooses one.
Overrides share the exact signature; the JVM chooses by the object's class.
Static methods and fields never dispatch; they bind to the declared type.
Replace `instanceof` chains with overrides so new types need no caller edits.

steps.caption: `p` is declared as `Payment`. The compiler looks only at methods `Payment` declares or inherits.
It picks `fee(long)` and writes that signature into the bytecode. Overloads are settled here, for good.
At run time the JVM reads the object's real class: `CardPayment`, not `Payment`.
It searches `CardPayment` for `fee(long)` first, then walks up to parents if missing.
The override in `CardPayment` runs. Same call, different body: that is dynamic dispatch.
`auditor.log(p)`: the overload is fixed from the argument's static type, `Payment`. The JVM dispatches on `auditor` only, never on `p`.

code.title: Which method runs?
code.caption: Five lookups on a `CardPayment`: only the overridden instance method follows the runtime class.

walk.text: Static type `Payment`, runtime class `CardPayment`. Every rule below hinges on this gap.
`fee` is overridden, so the JVM runs the `CardPayment` body.
These two `log` methods are overloads: same name, different parameter types.
The compiler picks the overload from the declared type, ignoring the object.
`p.kind()` is static: hidden, not overridden, so the declared type `Payment` decides.
Fields are hidden too. Reading `p.name` uses the `Payment` field.

code.title: Dispatch as a design tool
code.caption: Each ride computes its own fare, so callers never branch on type.

walk.text: The base validates shared state once and declares the abstract `fareCents`.
Each subclass overrides one method with its own pricing rule.
`totalFare` has no `instanceof` or `switch`. Dispatch picks the rule per object.
A new ride type is a new class. No caller changes: the Open/Closed Principle (OCP).
The new class still validates its own extra field.

pitfalls: Writing `equals(Money)` instead of `equals(Object)` overloads it; collections then ignore it.
Omitting `@Override`; a typo in the signature quietly becomes a new overload.
Expecting an overload to follow the runtime type; it follows the declared type.

quiz.q: `Point` declares `equals(Point)`, not `equals(Object)`. What does this print?
quiz.why: With static type `Point`, the compiler picks `equals(Point)`. With static type `Object`, it picks `equals(Object)`, never overridden, so identity decides.

takeaway: Compiler picks the signature; runtime class picks the body.

starters: How does the JVM find the override quickly at run time?
Can I make an overload pick by runtime type, like double dispatch?
Why can private and static methods not be overridden?
